title: Python Language & Systems Quiz
description: Examine Python execution models, generators, GIL implications, and asyncio concurrency.

questions.question: Why does Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) prevent CPU-bound tasks from running in parallel on multi-core systems when using the standard `threading` module?
options: Because operating system kernels only assign one hardware thread to Python processes.
Because the GIL permits only one native thread to execute Python bytecodes at any given time to protect CPython's internal memory management and reference counting.
Because Python functions cannot allocate memory across multiple CPU caches.
Because multithreading in Python is restricted to 32-bit architectures.
questions.explanation: CPython uses reference counting for garbage collection. The GIL is a mutual-exclusion lock that prevents multiple native threads from executing Python bytecodes concurrently, avoiding race conditions in reference counts. To achieve parallel CPU execution, you must use `multiprocessing` or free-threaded Python 3.13+.

questions.question: What will the following Python generator expression yield in terms of memory usage when processing 10 million records?
options: Around 800 Megabytes of RAM to store the array in memory.
Negligible memory (under 200 bytes) because the generator produces values lazily on-demand.
MemoryError crash immediately upon variable assignment.
10 Gigabytes of temporary disk swap space.
questions.explanation: Parentheses `(...)` create a generator expression rather than a list comprehension `[...]`. Generators evaluate lazily, producing numbers one at a time via the iterator protocol (`__next__`), using constant O(1) memory regardless of how many elements are iterated.
